stem: The two thigh bones (femurs), each of cross-sectional area \(10\,\text{cm}^2\) support the upper part of a human body of mass \(40\,\text{kg}\). Estimate the average pressure sustained by the femurs.
solution:
Total cross-sectional area of the femurs is \(A = 2 \times 10\,\text{cm}^2 = 20 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{m}^2\). The force acting on them is \(F = 40\,\text{kg wt} = 400\,\text{N}\) (taking \(g = 10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\)). This force is acting vertically down and hence, normally on the femurs. Thus, the average pressure is

\(P_{av} = \frac{F}{A} = 2 \times 10^{5}\,\text{N m}^{-2}\)

stem: What is the pressure on a swimmer \(10\,\text{m}\) below the surface of a lake?
solution:
Here \(h = 10\,\text{m}\) and \(\rho = 1000\,\text{kg m}^{-3}\). Take \(g = 10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\).

From Eq. (9.7)

\(P = P_a + \rho g h\)

\(= 1.01 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa} + 1000\,\text{kg m}^{-3} \times 10\,\text{m s}^{-2} \times 10\,\text{m}\)

\(= 2.01 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}\)

\(\approx 2\,\text{atm}\)

This is a 100% increase in pressure from surface level. At a depth of 1 km, the increase in pressure is 100 atm! Submarines are designed to withstand such enormous pressures.

stem: The density of the atmosphere at sea level is \(1.29\,\text{kg/m}^3\). Assume that it does not change with altitude. Then how high would the atmosphere extend?
solution:
We use Eq. (9.7)

\(\rho g h = 1.29\,\text{kg m}^{-3} \times 9.8\,\text{m s}^{2} \times h\,\text{m} = 1.01 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}\)

\(\therefore h = 7989\,\text{m} \approx 8\,\text{km}\)

In reality the density of air decreases with height. So does the value of \(g\). The atmospheric cover extends with decreasing pressure over 100 km. We should also note that the sea level atmospheric pressure is not always 760 mm of Hg. A drop in the Hg level by 10 mm or more is a sign of an approaching storm.
_note: PRINTED DEFECT (transcribed faithfully): the book prints the acceleration due to gravity as \(9.8\,\text{m s}^{2}\) with a POSITIVE exponent; it must be \(\text{m s}^{-2}\). Verified at 4x zoom on p-04 — the minus sign is clearly present on \(\text{kg m}^{-3}\) earlier in the SAME line and clearly absent here, so it is a dropped exponent sign, not a rendering artefact. The arithmetic is unaffected and confirms the intended value: \(1.01 \times 10^{5} / (1.29 \times 9.8) = 7989\,\text{m}\).

stem: At a depth of \(1000\,\text{m}\) in an ocean (a) what is the absolute pressure? (b) What is the gauge pressure? (c) Find the force acting on the window of area \(20\,\text{cm} \times 20\,\text{cm}\) of a submarine at this depth, the interior of which is maintained at sea-level atmospheric pressure. (The density of sea water is \(1.03 \times 10^{3}\,\text{kg m}^{-3}\), \(g = 10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\).)
solution:
Here \(h = 1000\,\text{m}\) and \(\rho = 1.03 \times 10^{3}\,\text{kg m}^{-3}\).

(a) From Eq. (9.6), absolute pressure

\(P = P_a + \rho g h\)

\(= 1.01 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa} + 1.03 \times 10^{3}\,\text{kg m}^{-3} \times 10\,\text{m s}^{-2} \times 1000\,\text{m}\)

\(= 104.01 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}\)

\(\approx 104\,\text{atm}\)

(b) Gauge pressure is \(P - P_a = \rho g h = P_g\)

\(P_g = 1.03 \times 10^{3}\,\text{kg m}^{-3} \times 10\,\text{ms}^{2} \times 1000\,\text{m}\)

\(= 103 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}\)

\(\approx 103\,\text{atm}\)

(c) The pressure outside the submarine is \(P = P_a + \rho g h\) and the pressure inside it is \(P_a\). Hence, the net pressure acting on the window is gauge pressure, \(P_g = \rho g h\). Since the area of the window is \(A = 0.04\,\text{m}^2\), the force acting on it is

\(F = P_g A = 103 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa} \times 0.04\,\text{m}^2 = 4.12 \times 10^{5}\,\text{N}\)
_note: PRINTED DEFECT (transcribed faithfully): in part (b) the book prints \(10\,\text{ms}^{2}\) with a POSITIVE exponent; it must be \(\text{m s}^{-2}\). Verified at 5x zoom on p-05 — the minus is clearly present on \(\text{kg m}^{-3}\) in the same line and absent here. The book is INTERNALLY INCONSISTENT: part (a) of this same example prints \(10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\) correctly, which is what identifies this as a typesetting slip rather than intent. The stated result \(103 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}\) confirms \(g = 10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\) was used.

stem: Two syringes of different cross-sections (without needles) filled with water are connected with a tightly fitted rubber tube filled with water. Diameters of the smaller piston and larger piston are \(1.0\,\text{cm}\) and \(3.0\,\text{cm}\) respectively. (a) Find the force exerted on the larger piston when a force of \(10\,\text{N}\) is applied to the smaller piston. (b) If the smaller piston is pushed in through \(6.0\,\text{cm}\), how much does the larger piston move out?
solution:
(a) Since pressure is transmitted undiminished throughout the fluid,

\(F_2 = \frac{A_2}{A_1} F_1 = \frac{\pi\left(3/2 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}\right)^2}{\pi\left(1/2 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}\right)^2} \times 10\,\text{N} = 90\,\text{N}\)

(b) Water is considered to be perfectly incompressible. Volume covered by the movement of smaller piston inwards is equal to volume moved outwards due to the larger piston.

\(L_1 A_1 = L_2 A_2\)

\(L_2 = \frac{A_1}{A_2} L_1 = \frac{\pi\left(1/2 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}\right)^2}{\pi\left(3/2 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}\right)^2} \times 6 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}\)

\(\simeq 0.67 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m} = 0.67\,\text{cm}\)

Note, atmospheric pressure is common to both pistons and has been ignored.

stem: In a car lift compressed air exerts a force \(F_1\) on a small piston having a radius of \(5.0\,\text{cm}\). This pressure is transmitted to a second piston of radius \(15\,\text{cm}\) (Fig 9.7). If the mass of the car to be lifted is \(1350\,\text{kg}\), calculate \(F_1\). What is the pressure necessary to accomplish this task? (\(g = 9.8\,\text{ms}^{-2}\)).
solution:
Since pressure is transmitted undiminished throughout the fluid,

\(F_1 = \frac{A_1}{A_2} F_2 = \frac{\pi(5 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m})^2}{\pi(15 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m})^2}\left(1350\,\text{kg} \times 9.8\,\text{m s}^{-2}\right)\)

\(= 1470\,\text{N}\)

\(\approx 1.5 \times 10^{3}\,\text{N}\)

The air pressure that will produce this force is

\(P = \frac{F_1}{A_1} = \frac{1.5 \times 10^{3}\,\text{N}}{\pi\left(5 \times 10^{-2}\right)^2\,\text{m}} = 1.9 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}\)

This is almost double the atmospheric pressure.
_note: TWO PRINTED DEFECTS (both transcribed faithfully). (1) STALE CROSS-REFERENCE: the stem cites "(Fig 9.7)", but Fig 9.7 in this chapter is "The meaning of streamlines" (p-06/p-07); the hydraulic-lift schematic this example describes is Fig 9.6(b) on p-05. Verified at 4x zoom on p-06 and against the Fig 9.7 caption on the same page and its reuse on p-07. (2) In the final pressure expression the denominator prints \(\pi(5 \times 10^{-2})^2\,\text{m}\) with the unit \(\text{m}\) OUTSIDE the square, so as printed the area carries units of m rather than m^2. Values are unaffected.

stem: A fully loaded Boeing aircraft has a mass of \(3.3 \times 10^{5}\,\text{kg}\). Its total wing area is \(500\,\text{m}^2\). It is in level flight with a speed of \(960\,\text{km/h}\). (a) Estimate the pressure difference between the lower and upper surfaces of the wings (b) Estimate the fractional increase in the speed of the air on the upper surface of the wing relative to the lower surface. [The density of air is \(\rho = 1.2\,\text{kg m}^{-3}\)]
solution:
(a) The weight of the Boeing aircraft is balanced by the upward force due to the pressure difference

\(\Delta P \; A = 3.3 \times 10^{5}\,\text{kg} \times 9.8\)

\(\Delta P = (3.3 \times 10^{5}\,\text{kg} \times 9.8\,\text{m s}^{-2}) / 500\,\text{m}^2\)

\(= 6.5 \times 10^{3}\,\text{N m}^{-2}\)

(b) We ignore the small height difference between the top and bottom sides in Eq. (9.12). The pressure difference between them is then

\(\Delta P = \frac{\rho}{2}\left(v_2^2 - v_1^2\right)\)

where \(v_2\) is the speed of air over the upper surface and \(v_1\) is the speed under the bottom surface.

\(\left(v_2 - v_1\right) = \frac{2\Delta P}{\rho\left(v_2 + v_1\right)}\)

Taking the average speed

\(v_{av} = (v_2 + v_1)/2 = 960\,\text{km/h} = 267\,\text{m s}^{-1}\),

we have

\(\left(v_2 - v_1\right)/v_{av} = \frac{\Delta P}{\rho v_{av}^2} \approx 0.08\)

The speed above the wing needs to be only 8 % higher than that below.
_note: PRINTED ODDITY (transcribed faithfully): the first line of the answer prints \(\Delta P \; A = 3.3 \times 10^{5}\,\text{kg} \times 9.8\) with no multiplication sign between \(\Delta P\) and \(A\), and with the units of \(g\) omitted from the right-hand side. The very next line supplies them correctly.

stem: A metal block of area \(0.10\,\text{m}^2\) is connected to a \(0.010\,\text{kg}\) mass via a string that passes over an ideal pulley (considered massless and frictionless), as in Fig. 9.13. A liquid with a film thickness of \(0.30\,\text{mm}\) is placed between the block and the table. When released the block moves to the right with a constant speed of \(0.085\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). Find the coefficient of viscosity of the liquid.
solution:
The metal block moves to the right because of the tension in the string. The tension \(T\) is equal in magnitude to the weight of the suspended mass m. Thus, the shear force \(F\) is

\(F = T = mg = 0.010\,\text{kg} \times 9.8\,\text{m s}^{-2} = 9.8 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{N}\)

Shear stress on the fluid \(= F/A = \frac{9.8 \times 10^{-2}}{0.10}\,\text{N/m}^2\)

Strain rate \(= \frac{v}{l} = \frac{0.085}{0.30 \times 10^{-3}}\)

\(h = \frac{\text{stress}}{\text{strain rate}}\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

\(= \frac{(9.8 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{N})\,(0.30 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m})}{(0.085\,\text{m s}^{-1})\,(0.10\,\text{m}^2)}\)

\(= 3.46 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{Pa s}\)
_note: TWO PRINTED DEFECTS (both transcribed faithfully). (1) WRONG SYMBOL: the book sets the coefficient of viscosity as an italic Latin \(h\) in the line \(h = \text{stress}/\text{strain rate}\); the chapter's symbol is Greek \(\eta\) (Eq. 9.16, Table 9.2, SUMMARY item 9 and the p-19 symbols table all use \(\eta\)). Verified at 6x zoom on p-12 — it is unambiguously a Latin h. This is the classic Symbol-font eta mapping to Latin 'h' reaching print. (2) SPURIOUS UNIT: that same line carries a trailing \(\text{s}^{-1}\), which does not belong — strain rate already carries s^-1 in the denominator, and the quoted result \(3.46 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{Pa s}\) is correct without it (stress \(0.98\,\text{N m}^{-2}\) divided by strain rate \(283.3\,\text{s}^{-1}\)).

stem: The terminal velocity of a copper ball of radius \(2.0\,\text{mm}\) falling through a tank of oil at \(20^\circ\text{C}\) is \(6.5\,\text{cm s}^{-1}\). Compute the viscosity of the oil at \(20^\circ\text{C}\). Density of oil is \(1.5 \times 10^{3}\,\text{kg m}^{-3}\), density of copper is \(8.9 \times 10^{3}\,\text{kg m}^{-3}\).

The lower end of a capillary tube of diameter \(2.00\,\text{mm}\) is dipped \(8.00\,\text{cm}\) below the surface of water in a beaker. What is the pressure required in the tube in order to blow a hemispherical bubble at its end in water? The surface tension of water at temperature of the experiments is \(7.30 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{Nm}^{-1}\). 1 atmospheric pressure \(= 1.01 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}\), density of water \(= 1000\,\text{kg/m}^3\), \(g = 9.80\,\text{m s}^{-2}\). Also calculate the excess pressure.
solution:
The excess pressure in a bubble of gas in a liquid is given by \(2S/r\), where \(S\) is the surface tension of the liquid-gas interface. You should note there is only one liquid surface in this case. (For a bubble of liquid in a gas, there are two liquid surfaces, so the formula for excess pressure in that case is \(4S/r\).) The radius of the bubble is r. Now the pressure outside the bubble \(P_o\) equals atmospheric pressure plus the pressure due to \(8.00\,\text{cm}\) of water column. That is

\(P_o = (1.01 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa} + 0.08\,\text{m} \times 1000\,\text{kg m}^{-3} \times 9.80\,\text{m s}^{-2})\)

\(= 1.01784 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}\)

Therefore, the pressure inside the bubble is

\(P_i = P_o + 2S/r\)

\(= 1.01784 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa} + (2 \times 7.3 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{Pa m}/10^{-3}\,\text{m})\)

\(= (1.01784 + 0.00146) \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}\)

\(= 1.02 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}\)

where the radius of the bubble is taken to be equal to the radius of the capillary tube, since the bubble is hemispherical! (The answer has been rounded off to three significant figures.) The excess pressure in the bubble is \(146\,\text{Pa}\).
